doc.title: Michael Weiss interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 22, 2021

title: Repetition and sequence in composition and solos
summary: Good songs and solos repeat and vary material before new information; Metheny's remark about non sequiturs.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: It was used as sort of a button, the end, they lived happily ever after, on to the next. Yeah. It’s a little marker. A melodic marker. Yeah. Using and re-using your material, repetition or sequencing is the hallmark of a good song. And it can be referred to as a hook, but any — I talk about this, I recently did an online composition and arranging master class called “Getting More Out of Your Tunes” where almost any good song has some repetition in it, has some sequencing. You can’t just have a continuous run-on sentence of new material without ever repeating anything because I think the listener will turn off. But if you just repeat something, you can even change it when you repeat it, a variation of some sort, but any type of sequence, a sequence, repetition, whatever you call it, when a listener hears something a second time it’s like then they get it so that now they’re ready to hear new information. But if you’re only giving out new information all the time then you can’t process it. I went to the store, I looked at computers, I looked at monitors, then I went and had a coffee. So you know what I’m saying? It’s like you’re ready for something new. And I think a good solo tells a story in a similar kind of way. You can’t just have a whole series of non sequiturs. There’s a great interview with Pat Metheny I saw recently where he talked about how so many young improvisers today, their solos are just made up of non sequiturs. And it’s so true.
